title: Cybersecurity foundations and the CIA triad
subtitle: Understand confidentiality, integrity, availability, assets, threats, weaknesses, impact and layered controls.
description: Understand confidentiality, integrity, availability, assets, threats, weaknesses, impact and layered controls. Guided explanations, six original visual diagrams, safe practice, trusted resource links, worked examples and a randomized quiz.

blocks.text: Lesson 1 — Cybersecurity foundations and the CIA triad

LEARNING OUTCOME
Understand confidentiality, integrity, availability, assets, threats, weaknesses, impact and layered controls.

Safety rule: work only with devices, accounts and training applications you own or have explicit written permission to assess. Use synthetic information. A public system or a suspicious person is not permission.

Cybersecurity keeps information and systems trustworthy while allowing the right people to use them. Confidentiality limits disclosure; integrity protects correctness; availability keeps required services usable. These aims can conflict: a strict access rule may protect confidentiality while accidentally blocking legitimate work. Begin with the business purpose, the asset, and the acceptable risk rather than buying tools first.

blocks.text: A threat is a possible cause of harm; a vulnerability is a weakness that could be used or triggered; impact is the consequence; a control reduces likelihood or impact. A bug or alert is not proof that a breach occurred, and an alert is not proof a particular person is responsible. Separate verified facts, hypotheses and conclusions.

blocks.caption: Visual 3/6 — Threat path. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 4/6 — Layered controls. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: Start with an inventory, unique accounts, MFA, timely updates, protected and tested backups, secure configuration, monitoring and a response plan. Assign an owner to each control and test whether it works. Security maturity is built by making fundamental safeguards repeatable and reviewing them, not by assuming one product stops every threat.

blocks.text: Practice checklist: (1) read the lab rules, (2) use fabricated data or an isolated training target, (3) predict what the control should do, (4) test one small condition, (5) save only minimal evidence, and (6) explain the defensive follow-up. Stop and ask the owner if any target or action is outside the approved scope.

blocks.question: Which security property means authorized users can access a service when needed?
blocks.explanation: Availability concerns reliable access to needed services.
blocks.hint: Use the lesson definitions and authorization boundary to reason through the options.

blocks.question: Is an alert proof that a person caused a breach?
options: Only if the alert is red
Only when the server is old
blocks.explanation: An alert is a signal to investigate, not proof of attribution.
blocks.hint: Use the lesson definitions and authorization boundary to reason through the options.

blocks.question: Which approach better protects private information?
options: Use synthetic data and collect only necessary, authorized evidence
Copy all customer records for convenience
blocks.explanation: Data minimization and redaction reduce privacy and exposure risks.
blocks.hint: Use the lesson definitions and authorization boundary to reason through the options.

blocks.question: What is a sound step after applying a fix?
options: Retest the same authorized condition and document the result
blocks.explanation: Retesting verifies the correction and preserves a useful record.
blocks.hint: Use the lesson definitions and authorization boundary to reason through the options.

blocks.question: What should happen when a target is outside scope?
options: Stop and ask the owner to clarify permission
blocks.explanation: Scope is a boundary; do not proceed without permission.
